pages.title: The Boats
pages.content:
The Boats

Five independent day boats land at Quay 2 from 04:40, one for each day we open: the Morwen on Tuesday, the Ellie Rose on Wednesday, the Saoirse on Thursday, the Two Sisters on Friday and the Kestrel on Saturday.

pages.title: The Counter
pages.content:
The Counter

The board changes with the boats. Gilt-head bream is €24.00 / kg, line-caught mackerel €14.00 / kg, sea bass fillets €42.00 / kg and cleaned squid €22.00 / kg. Filleting, scaling and gutting on any whole fish is free.

pages.title: Cut to Order
pages.content:
Cut to Order

Choose a whole fish on the ice, tell us how you will cook it, and we cut while you wait, about six minutes a fish. Everything is wrapped in waxed paper, and heads and frames are bagged for stock if you want them.

pages.title: The Day
pages.content:
The Day

Boats tie up at 04:40, the doors open at 07:30, phone orders close at 10:00, the trim run leaves at 12:00 and the ice is washed down at 18:00.

pages.title: Kitchens
pages.content:
Kitchens

Every day the clean trim and frames go to three neighbourhood kitchens: Linnet bistro, Harrowmouth Primary School and The Oxbow Community Kitchen.

pages.title: About
pages.content:
About

Kaimon Fishmongers was founded in 2009 by Maren Holt in a former net store at 4 Quay Row, Harrowmouth, and is named after the old sea gate at the end of the row.

pages.title: People
pages.content:
People

Seven of us work the quay and the counter, from Maren Holt, who buys on the quay, to Hugo Lindqvist, our apprentice cutter.

pages.title: Visit
pages.content:
Visit

4 Quay Row, Harrowmouth. Open Tuesday to Friday 07:30–18:00 and Saturday 07:00–14:00; closed Sunday and Monday. The harbour bus stop is three minutes on foot.

pages.title: Order
pages.content:
Order

Phone orders are taken 07:30–10:00 on 0100 555 0409 for same-day cuts, with pickup from 12:00. You can also write to counter@kaimonfish.example.

pages.title: The Landing List
pages.content:
The Landing List

Every Monday at 17:00 we send a three-minute note on which boats are expected and what they will likely bring.

pages.title: Privacy
pages.content:
Privacy

This sample site stores nothing about you. The email form opens your own mail app and sends nothing by itself.

posts.title: How to tell a fish came in this morning
posts.excerpt: Clear eyes, red gills and a clean smell of the sea: three things to look at on the ice before you choose.
posts.content:
Walk up to the ice board before you decide what you want for dinner. A fish that came in this morning looks the part: the eye is clear and full, not sunken or clouded, and the gills under the cover are a deep, bright red rather than brown or grey.

Then lean in. Fresh fish smells of the sea, cool and clean, never sharp. Press the flank gently with a finger; the flesh should spring back at once and the scales should lie flat and shine.

If you are not sure, ask. Idris will lift any fish off the ice, turn it over and show you what he is looking at, and he will cut it for you in about six minutes once you have chosen.

posts.title: What the Thursday boat brings in October
posts.excerpt: The Saoirse fishes pots off the headland, and in October the brown crabs are heavy and full.
posts.content:
The Saoirse lands at Quay 2 on Thursdays with the pots she hauled the evening before. In October the brown crabs are at their heaviest, and the skipper sorts them on the quay so that only the full ones come up the steps to the shop.

We sell them live or cooked and dressed, at €9.50 each for the dressed ones. Lobster comes in smaller numbers and is gone early, so if you want one, ring on Wednesday afternoon and we will put it aside.

The empty pots stack on the quay until Saturday, when the Kestrel takes the same berth for her hand-dived scallops and rope mussels.

posts.title: A stock from frames: what the kitchens make with our trim
posts.excerpt: Every day the frames and heads leave the counter for three kitchens. This is what they do with them.
posts.content:
After the cutting is done, the frames and heads from the day's fish are washed, bagged and kept on ice. At noon Anjali takes them on the trim run to three neighbourhood kitchens.

At Linnet, the cooks simmer the frames gently for twenty minutes with a leek and a few peppercorns, strain the stock clear and use it for the fish pie. The school kitchen turns boneless mackerel trim into fishcakes, and the Oxbow Community Kitchen makes a bream and bass broth for its Sunday lunch.

You can take frames home too. Ask for a stock bag at the counter, about 1.5 kg, for €4.00, and start with cold water.
